tool_calls.result:
Loaded rent_increased. Its instructions:

# Rent increased

Rests on 83.46 (rent, tenancies with no set term), 83.43 (what rent is, good faith), 83.57 (ending a tenancy with no set term), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.425 (local rules), 83.56 (unpaid rent, rent paid, notices), 83.60 (if sued), 83.55 and 83.54 (damages, suits), 83.44 and 83.45 (good faith, unfair clauses), 83.48 (attorney fees), 83.51 and 83.491 (trash, a fee in place of a deposit), 83.59 and 83.67 (no lockout), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets all its readings, and you choose none.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- Part II has no section that sets how much notice a rent increase needs, and none that limits how much rent may go up. Say so plainly when asked. Never state a notice period or a cap as the law.
- Local rules: "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." (83.425), and the section supersedes local rules on matters including "fees charged by the landlord; or notice requirements." (83.425). The stored text holds no local rent rule. Never apply one from memory.
- Rent paid through a program (a voucher, public housing): the program's own rules are not stored. Say they may limit this, and that they are outside this tool.
- The increase comes with an offer to renew, or the tenant would rather leave: load lease_ending too.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the rent, the term, any clause on the rent changing, how the lease may be changed, any charges, staying after the end, and how notices go to the landlord. Quote each clause and cite it.

- **Rent steps set in the lease from the start** (so much until a date, then more): that is the lease's rent, not an increase. Say so.
- **A clause letting the landlord raise the rent during the term:** set the increase beside the clause's conditions (how much notice, how it is given, how much, how often). If it gives a number of days N: the last day to give notice for the start date named is count_days(new_rent_starts, -N), and the earliest start from the notice given is count_days(increase_delivered, N). All conditions met: the rent goes up as the lease says; say so plainly. Any not met: the clause does not support this increase on these terms; say so plainly and go to option 1. A clause with no limit at all: say what it says, that it carries "an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement." (83.44), and that whether it is unfair enough to be "unconscionable" (83.45(1)) is for a court.
- **A new charge** (an amenity fee, a trash fee): the same questions as for rent. The lease provides it: owed as the lease says. It does not: during a set term the landlord cannot add it alone, any more than it can raise the rent. A fee counts as rent only if it is "designated as rent in a written rental agreement." (83.43(12)). That matters because a demand under 83.56(3) and the registry under 83.60(2) speak of rent.
  - Trash: in a unit other than a single-family home or duplex, "Garbage removal and outside receptacles therefor." (83.51(2)(a)) falls to the landlord "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)), though the rental agreement may put the charges on the tenant (83.51(2)(e)).
  - A fee in place of a security deposit: "The amount of the fee, which may not be increased during the term of the rental agreement." (83.491(4)(a)).

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- new_rent: the new amount. increase_delivered: the date word of it reached them, and how it came (handed over, mail, portal, text, spoken). new_rent_starts: the date it is said to start.
- lease_end_date: the date the lease ends, if it has one. period_end: the last day of the rent period before the new rent starts. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- agreed: whether they signed anything or said yes. paid_new_rent: whether they have paid the new amount, for which months, and what they knew about the lease when they paid.
- complaint_date: the date of any complaint before the increase, and what it was. others_rent: what they know about other tenants' rent.
- rent_demand: any written demand for rent, and its date. eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served.

## Which kind of increase

Settle this first. With a set end date, call count_days(lease_end_date, 0) and set new_rent_starts beside the date it gives.

- A set end date, and the new rent starts on or before it: option 1.
- A set end date, and the new rent starts after it: option 2.
- No set end date, or the tenant stayed on after a set term with the landlord's permission: option 3. With no term stated, "the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). Stayed on without permission, or in doubt: load lease_ending too.

Any kind: option 4 if the tenant complained first, and the two parts after it if they fit.

## Option 1: during a set term

Part II has no section that lets a landlord raise the rent during a set term. The rent is what the lease says. Quote the rent clause and any clause on changing the lease.

1. **No clause allows it** (see "What the lease adds").
2. **The tenant did not agree.**
   - They signed a change: the rent is what they signed, if it meets the lease's clause on changes.
   - They said yes without signing: not settled whether that changes the rent. One: a rental agreement can include an "oral agreement for a duration of less than 1 year" (83.43(13)). The other: a lease clause requiring a signed change still governs.
   - They paid it without signing: see "If the tenant already paid it".

Both met: the landlord cannot change the rent alone before the lease ends. Say so plainly. The tenant keeps paying the lease's rent, in full and on time, and can tell the landlord in writing that they do not agree, quoting the rent clause and sending it the way the lease's notice clause says. It helps to keep the letter, the lease, and proof of each payment. Say the risk too: see "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent". The landlord can ask for more when the term ends (option 2).

## Option 2: a higher rent for a new term

Part II names no right to renew at the same rent and no limit on what a landlord may ask for a new term. Say so plainly. The lease's rent stands through lease_end_date whatever the offer says. From there:

- **Agree:** the new rent starts with the new term. Say what they should read before signing: the rent, the term, and any new charge.
- **Leave at the end:** load lease_ending for any notice the lease asks for.
- **Stay without agreeing:** load lease_ending. Staying without permission can mean "double the amount of rent due" (83.58). Read the lease's clause on staying after the end; if it makes the tenancy month to month, say what it says, and option 3 applies from then.

## Option 3: no set end date

Part II sets no notice for this and does not say a landlord may change the rent alone, so what an increase takes is not settled. Give all three readings and choose none. Quote any lease clause on signed changes.

- One: a landlord that can end the tenancy only on 83.57's notice can change the rent only with the same notice, written and delivered a way 83.56(4) names, for month to month "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)).
- Two: no section sets a notice, so none in particular is needed, and the tenant can pay it or leave.
- Three: 83.57 only lets a party end the tenancy, so the rent changes only if the tenant agrees, and a landlord that wants more must end the tenancy on that notice and offer new terms. A lease clause requiring a signed change points this way.

The date: count_days(period_end, -N), with N from 83.57: 30 for month to month (83.57(3)), and for other rent periods the number in 83.57(1), (2), or (4). Set increase_delivered beside it. The ways 83.56(4) names are mailing, a true copy by hand, e-mail under the signed addendum in 83.505(1), or, if the tenant is away, a copy left at the home.

- In writing, a way named, and on or before that date: in time under readings one and two. Say so plainly. Under reading three the letter alone still does not change the rent.
- Later than that, or spoken, or by text or portal: not good for that date under reading one, enough under reading two, and no change under reading three. Whether a late notice works for the next period under reading one is not settled, as lease_ending says of a late notice to end a tenancy; its date is count_days(next_period_end, -N).

Under every reading the landlord may end the tenancy on that notice: it "may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57), and no reason is named. Say so, so the tenant knows what refusing can lead to.

The tenant's choices:

- Pay the new rent. See "If the tenant already paid it" for what paying may mean.
- Pay the old rent and say in writing why. See "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent".
- End the tenancy: load lease_ending. The last day to give notice is count_days(period_end, -N), or count_days(next_period_end, -N) if that has passed.

## Option 4: retaliation

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)).

All of these must be met.

1. **Something the tenant did first.** "Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where:" (83.64(1)) they complained to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), took part in a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), complained to the landlord under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), ended a lease as a servicemember (83.64(1)(d)), paid rent to an association after its demand (83.64(1)(e)), or used fair housing rights (83.64(1)(f)). Fair housing law itself is outside this tool. Another step, like an ordinary repair request: not settled. One: the list is only examples, so it can count. The other: it counts only if it is like the named ones, and a request that says nothing about ending the lease is not 83.56(1)'s complaint.
2. **Good faith.** "In order for the tenant to raise the defense of retaliatory conduct, the tenant must have acted in good faith." (83.64(1)). "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). Applying that is for a court.
3. **Treated differently.** "“Discrimination” under this section means that a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)). Set what they know of other tenants' rent beside the words. The same increase for everyone points against it; say so plainly. If they do not know, say that is the fact to find out.
4. **Primarily because of the complaint.** This is the landlord's motive, for a court. An increase that followed a complaint is not retaliation for that reason alone. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

What it gives: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)), unless "the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)). So not paying the new rent can weaken it; say so.

What the tenant can do about an increase alone, before any case: not settled. One: 83.64(2) makes it only a defense, so there is nothing to raise until a case. The other: 83.64(1) makes the increase unlawful, "Any right or duty declared in this part is enforceable by civil action." (83.54), and a party may recover damages for a failure to comply with "this part" (83.55).

## If the tenant already paid it

"if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).

Ask what they knew when they paid, and set it beside "actual knowledge" (83.56(5)(a)). Whether paying a raised rent gives up the extra, or changes the rent from then on, is not settled. One: paying with knowledge gives up a suit over those months and may show the tenant agreed. The other: an increase the lease never allowed is not rent "due" (83.43(12)), a clause requiring a signed change still stands, and the extra can be claimed under 83.55, with each later month a "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool; do not total them.

## If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent

- **A written demand.** "If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(3)). This tool does not count those days; the demand states them. Say not to ignore it.
- **Taking the old rent.** A landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). So taking it does not mean the landlord gave in. "If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must:" (83.56(5)(a)) give a receipt with the date, the amount, and the balance before filing; or put the amount in the court's registry on filing; or post a new 3-day notice (83.56(5)(a)). Whether the lease's rent is "partial" at all is the dispute.
- **No court case, no removal.** "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)).
- **A case filed.** Say this first. The tenant must pay into the registry "the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon." (83.60(2)). When the amount is what they dispute, the motion is the way to say so: "If a motion to determine rent is filed, documentation in support of the allegation that the rent as alleged in the complaint is in error is required." (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits "only that portion of the full rent for which they are responsible" (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)).
- **Defenses.** The tenant "may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable, that he or she may have, including the defense of retaliatory conduct in accordance with s. 83.64" (83.60(1)(a)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating a notice period or a cap for rent increases as the law.
- Saying a landlord may raise the rent during a set term with no clause and no agreement, or calling the lease's own rent steps an increase.
- Treating 83.57's 30 days as settled for an increase, saying flatly that no notice is needed, or saying flatly that a letter alone changes the rent with no set end date.
- Saying an increase is retaliation because it followed a complaint, or leaving out good faith or being treated differently.
- Telling a tenant they can stop paying rent altogether, explaining a case without 83.60(2), or giving a calendar date for its 5 days.
- Applying a local rent rule from memory.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

answer:
**Short answer:** Florida's landlord-tenant law has no cap on rent increases, and it sets no notice period for one. Whether the letter alone raises your rent is not settled, because your lease says changes must be signed. On retaliation, the same letter went to every unit. The law requires you to have been treated differently from other tenants, so that points against retaliation. You haven't agreed to anything, and you can end the tenancy if you don't want the new rent. One thing would help me: did your January repair request say anything about ending the lease or moving out if the faucet wasn't fixed?

DETAILS

### Does Florida limit rent increases or set a notice period for one?
- Part II of the statute has no section that caps how much rent can go up. It also has no section that says how much notice an increase needs.
- Local rules can't fill that gap. Under 83.425, "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." The stored text holds no local rent rule.
- If a voucher or other program pays part of your rent, that program's rules may limit increases. Those rules are outside this tool.

### Did the letter raise your rent?
This is not settled. Your lease is month to month (lease §3), so there is no set end date. Under 83.46(2), the length of the tenancy is "determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." There are three readings.
- **Reading one:** A landlord can change the rent only with the same notice it would need to end the tenancy. For month to month, that is "not less than 30 days' notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)). The notice must be written and delivered a way 83.56(4) allows.
  - Your letter was in writing and handed to you on February 20. 83.56(4) allows "delivering a true copy."
  - The last day to give notice for an April 1 start was March 1, 2026. That date has not passed, so your notice was in time.
- **Reading two:** No section sets a notice, so none in particular is needed. You can pay the new rent or leave. Under this reading the increase also stands.
- **Reading three:** 83.57 only lets either side end the tenancy. The rent changes only if you agree. A landlord who wants more must end the tenancy on proper notice and offer new terms.
  - Lease §10 points this way: the lease "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant." You told me you did not agree.

Under every reading, your landlord can end a month-to-month tenancy with written notice under 83.57. The statute names no reason. So refusing the new rent could lead to a termination notice.

### Is this retaliation?
Several things must all be true under 83.64.
- **Something you did first.** The statute lists examples. One is a complaint to the landlord under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)). That kind of complaint is a written notice that names the problem and says you intend to end the lease if it isn't fixed. A portal repair request about a dripping faucet may not be that.
  - It is not settled whether an ordinary repair request counts. One reading is that the list is only examples, so it can count. The other is that it counts only if it is like the named examples.
  - This is why I asked what your request said.
- **Good faith.** You must have acted in good faith, which means "honesty in fact" (83.43(8)). A court would decide that.
- **Different treatment.** 83.64(4) says "Discrimination" means "a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged." That is "a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." You told me every unit got the same letter and the same percent. That points strongly against retaliation.
- **Motive.** The increase must be "primarily because the landlord is retaliating." A court decides motive. An increase that came after a complaint is not retaliation for that reason alone. Your complaint was January 20, 2026, and the letter was February 20, 2026.

Under 83.64(2), retaliation is raised as a defense "in any action brought against him or her for possession." It does not apply if the landlord proves good cause, such as "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)). It is not settled whether you can act on an increase alone, before any eviction case.
- One reading is that 83.64(2) makes it only a defense, so there is nothing to raise until a case is filed.
- The other reading is that 83.64(1) makes the increase unlawful, and 83.54 and 83.55 allow a civil action and damages for failing to comply with the part.

### What are your choices?
- **Pay the new rent.** If you pay with actual knowledge of a problem, you may give up a claim over those payments (83.56(5)(a)). It may also be read as agreeing to the new rent. This is not settled.
- **Pay the old rent and explain in writing.** Lease §7 says written notices to the landlord must be hand-delivered to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or sent there by certified mail. The risk is that the landlord treats the difference as unpaid rent. A written 3-day demand under 83.56(3) could follow, and you should not ignore it. Not paying the new rent can also weaken a retaliation defense.
- **End the tenancy.** The last day to give 30 days' notice before the end of the March period is March 1, 2026. If that date is missed, the last day for the April period is March 31, 2026. Both dates have not passed.

- **A clause letting the landlord raise the rent during the term:** set the increase beside the clause's conditions (how much notice, how it is given, how much, how often). Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- new_rent: the new amount. increase_delivered: the date word of it reached them, and how it came (handed over, mail, portal, text, spoken). new_rent_starts: the date it is said to start.
- lease_end_date: the date the lease ends, if it has one. period_end: the last day of the rent period before the new rent starts. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- agreed: whether they signed anything or said yes. paid_new_rent: whether they have paid the new amount, for which months, and what they knew about the lease when they paid.
- complaint_date: the date of any complaint before the increase, and what it was. others_rent: what they know about other tenants' rent.
- rent_demand: any written demand for rent, and its date. eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served.

## Which kind of increase

Settle this first. With a set end date, call count_days(lease_end_date, 0) and set new_rent_starts beside the date it gives.

- A set end date, and the new rent starts on or before it: option 1.
- A set end date, and the new rent starts after it: option 2.
- No set end date, or the tenant stayed on after a set term with the landlord's permission: option 3. With no term stated, "the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). Stayed on without permission, or in doubt: load lease_ending too.

Any kind: option 4 if the tenant complained first, and the two parts after it if they fit.

Part II has no section that lets a landlord raise the rent during a set term. The rent is what the lease says. Quote the rent clause and any clause on changing the lease.

1. **No clause allows it** (see "What the lease adds").

answer:
**Short answer:** Florida's landlord-tenant law doesn't say whether your landlord can raise your rent on this short notice, and that question is unsettled. It has no rule on how much notice a rent increase needs, and no cap on how much rent can go up. Your lease says it can be changed only in a signed writing, and you haven't signed or agreed to anything. You have a good argument that your rent is still $1,050 for now. Your landlord can also end a month-to-month tenancy on proper written notice, without giving a reason. Before the letter, did you complain to the landlord or to a government agency about anything, such as repairs?

DETAILS

### Does the law set a notice period or a cap for a rent increase?
No. Part II of the statute has no section on how much notice an increase needs, and none that limits the amount. Local rules can't fill that gap, because the state law says matters covered by this part are "preempted to the state" (83.425). I found no local rent rule in the stored text.

### What does your lease say?
- Rent is "$1,050.00 per month" (lease §4).
- The tenancy "continues from month to month until ended by Tenant or Landlord" (§3).
- Nothing in the lease lets the landlord raise the rent during the tenancy.
- The lease "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant" (§10).

### Did the letter change your rent? This is not settled.
The statute doesn't say. It gives three readings:
1. **Same notice as ending the tenancy.** Under 83.57(3), a month-to-month tenancy ends with "not less than 30 days' notice prior to the end of any monthly period." Under this reading, an increase needs that same notice. Your rent period ends March 31, and the last day to give 30 days' notice for it was March 1, which has passed. So the letter would be too late for April 1. A letter handed to you at the door is a delivery method 83.56(4) allows ("delivering a true copy"). Whether a late letter works for the next period, ending April 30, is also not settled. The last day to give notice for that period is March 31, and your letter came before that date. If it counts, the increase would start in May, not April.
2. **No set notice.** Because no section sets a notice period, the letter is enough. You would pay the new rent or leave.
3. **Only if you agree.** Section 83.57 only lets a party end the tenancy. Under this reading, the rent changes only if you agree. A landlord who wants more must end the tenancy on proper notice and offer new terms. Lease §10, which requires a signed change, points this way.

I can't tell you which reading a court would choose.

### What can your landlord do if you refuse?
Under any reading, your landlord can end the tenancy by written notice delivered as 83.56(4) describes. Section 83.57 names no required reason.

### What are your options?
- **Pay $1,050 and tell the landlord in writing why.** Quote lease §4 and §10 and say you did not agree. Lease §7 says to hand-deliver the letter to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send it there by certified mail. Keep a copy and proof of each payment.
  - **Risk:** your landlord may call the $150 difference unpaid rent. A written demand under 83.56(3) gives you 3 days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, to pay or leave. Don't ignore a demand like that. Accepting partial rent doesn't make your landlord give up its rights (83.56(5)(a)). Whether $1,050 counts as "partial" rent is the point you would be disputing.
  - **If a court case is filed:** you would have to pay the rent into the court registry, or file a motion to set the amount, within 5 days of being served, not counting Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays (83.60(2)). Missing that deadline can cost you every defense except payment.
- **Pay $1,200.** This may be read as you agreeing. Under 83.56(5)(a), paying with "actual knowledge" of your landlord's noncompliance can give up a claim over those payments. Whether that applies to a raised rent is also unsettled.
- **Leave.** Under 83.57(3), you would give written notice at least 30 days before the end of a monthly period. For the period ending April 30, the last day to give notice is March 31.

### Could this be retaliation?
The law bars a landlord from raising rent "discriminatorily" and "primarily because the landlord is retaliating" (83.64(1)). For that to apply, you must first have done something protected, such as complaining to a code agency or sending a written complaint to the landlord about the landlord's failure to meet its duties (83.64(1)(a), (c)). You must also have acted in good faith. Your rent must be treated differently from other tenants' (83.64(4)). The landlord's motive would be for a court to decide. If everyone got the same increase, that points against retaliation. I don't yet know whether you complained first, or what other tenants were charged.

Loaded rent_increased. Its instructions:

# Rent increased

Rests on 83.46 (rent, tenancies with no set term), 83.43 (what rent is, good faith), 83.57 (ending a tenancy with no set term), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.425 (local rules), 83.56 (unpaid rent, rent paid, notices), 83.60 (if sued), 83.55 and 83.54 (damages, suits), 83.44 and 83.45 (good faith, unfair clauses), 83.48 (attorney fees), 83.51 and 83.491 (trash, a fee in place of a deposit), 83.59 and 83.67 (no lockout), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets all its readings, and you choose none.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- Part II has no section that sets how much notice a rent increase needs, and none that limits how much rent may go up. Say so plainly when asked. Never state a notice period or a cap as the law.
- Local rules: "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." (83.425), and the section supersedes local rules on matters including "fees charged by the landlord; or notice requirements." (83.425). The stored text holds no local rent rule. Never apply one from memory.
- Rent paid through a program (a voucher, public housing): the program's own rules are not stored. Say they may limit this, and that they are outside this tool.
- The increase comes with an offer to renew, or the tenant would rather leave: load lease_ending too.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the rent, the term, any clause on the rent changing, how the lease may be changed, any charges, staying after the end, and how notices go to the landlord. Quote each clause and cite it.

- **Rent steps set in the lease from the start** (so much until a date, then more): that is the lease's rent, not an increase. Say so.
- **A clause letting the landlord raise the rent during the term:** set the increase beside the clause's conditions (how much notice, how it is given, how much, how often). If it gives a number of days N: the last day to give notice for the start date named is count_days(new_rent_starts, -N), and the earliest start from the notice given is count_days(increase_delivered, N). All conditions met: the rent goes up as the lease says; say so plainly. Any not met: the clause does not support this increase on these terms; say so plainly and go to option 1. A clause with no limit at all: say what it says, that it carries "an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement." (83.44), and that whether it is unfair enough to be "unconscionable" (83.45(1)) is for a court.
- **A new charge** (an amenity fee, a trash fee): the same questions as for rent. The lease provides it: owed as the lease says. It does not: during a set term the landlord cannot add it alone, any more than it can raise the rent. A fee counts as rent only if it is "designated as rent in a written rental agreement." (83.43(12)). That matters because a demand under 83.56(3) and the registry under 83.60(2) speak of rent.
  - Trash: in a unit other than a single-family home or duplex, "Garbage removal and outside receptacles therefor." (83.51(2)(a)) falls to the landlord "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)), though the rental agreement may put the charges on the tenant (83.51(2)(e)).
  - A fee in place of a security deposit: "The amount of the fee, which may not be increased during the term of the rental agreement." (83.491(4)(a)).

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- new_rent: the new amount. increase_delivered: the date word of it reached them, and how it came (handed over, mail, portal, text, spoken). new_rent_starts: the date it is said to start.
- lease_end_date: the date the lease ends, if it has one. period_end: the last day of the rent period before the new rent starts. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- agreed: whether they signed anything or said yes. paid_new_rent: whether they have paid the new amount, for which months, and what they knew about the lease when they paid.
- complaint_date: the date of any complaint before the increase, and what it was. others_rent: what they know about other tenants' rent.
- rent_demand: any written demand for rent, and its date. eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served.

## Which kind of increase

Settle this first. With a set end date, call count_days(lease_end_date, 0) and set new_rent_starts beside the date it gives.

- A set end date, and the new rent starts on or before it: option 1.
- A set end date, and the new rent starts after it: option 2.
- No set end date, or the tenant stayed on after a set term with the landlord's permission: option 3. With no term stated, "the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). Stayed on without permission, or in doubt: load lease_ending too.

Any kind: option 4 if the tenant complained first, and the two parts after it if they fit.

## Option 1: during a set term

Part II has no section that lets a landlord raise the rent during a set term. The rent is what the lease says. Quote the rent clause and any clause on changing the lease.

1. **No clause allows it** (see "What the lease adds").
2. **The tenant did not agree.**
   - They signed a change: the rent is what they signed, if it meets the lease's clause on changes.
   - They said yes without signing: not settled whether that changes the rent. One: a rental agreement can include an "oral agreement for a duration of less than 1 year" (83.43(13)). The other: a lease clause requiring a signed change still governs.
   - They paid it without signing: see "If the tenant already paid it".

Both met: the landlord cannot change the rent alone before the lease ends. Say so plainly. The tenant keeps paying the lease's rent, in full and on time, and can tell the landlord in writing that they do not agree, quoting the rent clause and sending it the way the lease's notice clause says. It helps to keep the letter, the lease, and proof of each payment. Say the risk too: see "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent". The landlord can ask for more when the term ends (option 2).

## Option 2: a higher rent for a new term

Part II names no right to renew at the same rent and no limit on what a landlord may ask for a new term. Say so plainly. The lease's rent stands through lease_end_date whatever the offer says. From there:

- **Agree:** the new rent starts with the new term. Say what they should read before signing: the rent, the term, and any new charge.
- **Leave at the end:** load lease_ending for any notice the lease asks for.
- **Stay without agreeing:** load lease_ending. Staying without permission can mean "double the amount of rent due" (83.58). Read the lease's clause on staying after the end; if it makes the tenancy month to month, say what it says, and option 3 applies from then.

## Option 3: no set end date

Part II sets no notice for this and does not say a landlord may change the rent alone, so what an increase takes is not settled. Give all three readings and choose none. Quote any lease clause on signed changes.

- One: a landlord that can end the tenancy only on 83.57's notice can change the rent only with the same notice, written and delivered a way 83.56(4) names, for month to month "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)).
- Two: no section sets a notice, so none in particular is needed, and the tenant can pay it or leave.
- Three: 83.57 only lets a party end the tenancy, so the rent changes only if the tenant agrees, and a landlord that wants more must end the tenancy on that notice and offer new terms. A lease clause requiring a signed change points this way.

The date: count_days(period_end, -N), with N from 83.57: 30 for month to month (83.57(3)), and for other rent periods the number in 83.57(1), (2), or (4). Set increase_delivered beside it. The ways 83.56(4) names are mailing, a true copy by hand, e-mail under the signed addendum in 83.505(1), or, if the tenant is away, a copy left at the home.

- In writing, a way named, and on or before that date: in time under readings one and two. Say so plainly. Under reading three the letter alone still does not change the rent.
- Later than that, or spoken, or by text or portal: not good for that date under reading one, enough under reading two, and no change under reading three. Whether a late notice works for the next period under reading one is not settled, as lease_ending says of a late notice to end a tenancy; its date is count_days(next_period_end, -N).

Under every reading the landlord may end the tenancy on that notice: it "may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57), and no reason is named. Say so, so the tenant knows what refusing can lead to.

The tenant's choices:

- Pay the new rent. See "If the tenant already paid it" for what paying may mean.
- Pay the old rent and say in writing why. See "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent".
- End the tenancy: load lease_ending. The last day to give notice is count_days(period_end, -N), or count_days(next_period_end, -N) if that has passed.

## Option 4: retaliation

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)).

All of these must be met.

1. **Something the tenant did first.** "Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where:" (83.64(1)) they complained to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), took part in a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), complained to the landlord under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), ended a lease as a servicemember (83.64(1)(d)), paid rent to an association after its demand (83.64(1)(e)), or used fair housing rights (83.64(1)(f)). Fair housing law itself is outside this tool. Another step, like an ordinary repair request: not settled. One: the list is only examples, so it can count. The other: it counts only if it is like the named ones, and a request that says nothing about ending the lease is not 83.56(1)'s complaint.
2. **Good faith.** "In order for the tenant to raise the defense of retaliatory conduct, the tenant must have acted in good faith." (83.64(1)). "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). Applying that is for a court.
3. **Treated differently.** "“Discrimination” under this section means that a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)). Set what they know of other tenants' rent beside the words. The same increase for everyone points against it; say so plainly. If they do not know, say that is the fact to find out.
4. **Primarily because of the complaint.** This is the landlord's motive, for a court. An increase that followed a complaint is not retaliation for that reason alone. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

What it gives: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)), unless "the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)). So not paying the new rent can weaken it; say so.

What the tenant can do about an increase alone, before any case: not settled. One: 83.64(2) makes it only a defense, so there is nothing to raise until a case. The other: 83.64(1) makes the increase unlawful, "Any right or duty declared in this part is enforceable by civil action." (83.54), and a party may recover damages for a failure to comply with "this part" (83.55).

## If the tenant already paid it

"if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).

Ask what they knew when they paid, and set it beside "actual knowledge" (83.56(5)(a)). Whether paying a raised rent gives up the extra, or changes the rent from then on, is not settled. One: paying with knowledge gives up a suit over those months and may show the tenant agreed. The other: an increase the lease never allowed is not rent "due" (83.43(12)), a clause requiring a signed change still stands, and the extra can be claimed under 83.55, with each later month a "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool; do not total them.

## If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent

- **A written demand.** "If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(3)). This tool does not count those days; the demand states them. Say not to ignore it.
- **Taking the old rent.** A landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). So taking it does not mean the landlord gave in. "If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must:" (83.56(5)(a)) give a receipt with the date, the amount, and the balance before filing; or put the amount in the court's registry on filing; or post a new 3-day notice (83.56(5)(a)). Whether the lease's rent is "partial" at all is the dispute.
- **No court case, no removal.** "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)).
- **A case filed.** Say this first. The tenant must pay into the registry "the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon." (83.60(2)). When the amount is what they dispute, the motion is the way to say so: "If a motion to determine rent is filed, documentation in support of the allegation that the rent as alleged in the complaint is in error is required." (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits "only that portion of the full rent for which they are responsible" (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)).
- **Defenses.** The tenant "may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable, that he or she may have, including the defense of retaliatory conduct in accordance with s. 83.64" (83.60(1)(a)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating a notice period or a cap for rent increases as the law.
- Saying a landlord may raise the rent during a set term with no clause and no agreement, or calling the lease's own rent steps an increase.
- Treating 83.57's 30 days as settled for an increase, saying flatly that no notice is needed, or saying flatly that a letter alone changes the rent with no set end date.
- Saying an increase is retaliation because it followed a complaint, or leaving out good faith or being treated differently.
- Telling a tenant they can stop paying rent altogether, explaining a case without 83.60(2), or giving a calendar date for its 5 days.
- Applying a local rent rule from memory.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

answer:
Yes, a complaint to code enforcement is the kind of thing Florida's retaliation law protects, and your facts fit part of that law. Whether your landlord raised the rent *primarily because of* your complaint is a question for a court, and nothing here settles it. It is also unsettled whether you can act on the increase now or only after your landlord files to evict you. Under your lease, the increase alone may not change your rent. The lease says it can be changed only in a writing both sides sign, and you did not agree.

I can't say what rent you will owe on April 1. That depends on which of three readings of the law a court follows. Until you know, don't stop paying rent. Not paying can weaken a retaliation defense.

Do you know whether the letter gives a reason for the increase, or mentions your mold complaint?

DETAILS

### Does the law cover your home?
Yes. You confirmed this is a private apartment complex, not school housing. Your lease (¶3) is month to month from August 1, 2025.

### Does Florida limit rent increases or set a notice period?
No. Part II of chapter 83 has no section that caps how much rent can go up. It also has no section that sets how much notice an increase needs. Section 83.425 says local rules on these matters are "preempted to the state." I have no local rent rule stored, so I'm not applying one.

### Did the letter change your rent?
Not settled. Your lease has no clause that lets the landlord raise the rent. Section 83.46(2) says that with no stated term, "the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." There are three readings:
1. **Same notice as ending the tenancy.** Under 83.57(3), a month-to-month tenancy ends with "not less than 30 days' notice prior to the end of any monthly period." On this reading, an increase needs the same written notice, delivered in a way 83.56(4) allows. The last day to give notice for an April 1 start is March 1, 2026. Your letter was handed to you at your door on February 20, in writing and before that date. So it would be in time on this reading.
2. **No particular notice needed.** No section sets one, so you can pay the new rent or leave. Your letter is enough on this reading too.
3. **A letter alone changes nothing.** Section 83.57 only lets either side end the tenancy. On this reading, the rent changes only if you agree. A landlord who wants more must end the tenancy on proper notice and offer new terms. Lease ¶10 points this way: "It may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant." You said you did not agree.

Under all three readings, your landlord can end a month-to-month tenancy by written notice under 83.57. That section names no reason.

### Does this count as retaliation?
Section 83.64(1) makes it unlawful to "discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent … primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." Each part is below.
- **Something you did first.** Yes. You complained to city code enforcement about mold on January 15, 2026. Section 83.64(1)(a) lists a complaint to a code agency as protected conduct.
- **Good faith.** You must have "acted in good faith" (83.64(1)). "Good faith" means "honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned" (83.43(8)). A court decides this. A real mold complaint points the right way.
- **Treated differently.** Section 83.64(4) says "Discrimination" means being "treated differently as to the rent charged." That is "a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." You say your neighbors' rent did not change. That is what they told you, so it helps to confirm it, for example with a copy of their notice or lease.
- **Primarily because of the complaint.** This is your landlord's motive, and a court decides it. A rent increase that came after a complaint is not retaliation for that reason alone. Other evidence would matter, such as a reason in the letter, a comment from staff, or the timing.

### What can you do about it now?
Not settled whether you can act before any eviction case.
- **One reading:** 83.64(2) makes retaliation a defense "in any action brought against him or her for possession." So there is nothing to raise until your landlord files.
- **The other reading:** 83.64(1) makes the increase unlawful, 83.54 says rights under this part are enforceable by civil action, and 83.55 allows damages for failure to comply with this part.

Steps that fit every reading:
- Keep the letter, the lease, your code enforcement complaint, and proof of every payment.
- You can tell your landlord in writing that you do not agree. Quote lease ¶10 and the rent in ¶4. Under lease ¶7, deliver it by hand to Suite A at 1840 SW 13th Street, or send it there by certified mail.
- Pay the rent you believe is due, in full and on time, and say in writing why. If your landlord treats that as unpaid rent, you could face a written 3-day demand under 83.56(3). Do not ignore a demand like that. If your landlord files a case, 83.60(2) requires you to pay rent into the court registry or file a motion about the amount within 5 days after being served, not counting weekends and holidays. Missing that waives your defenses other than payment.
- Under 83.59(3), your landlord cannot remove you without a court case. Under 83.67(2), your landlord cannot block your access to the apartment.
- If you pay the higher rent while knowing it may be unlawful, that may waive a claim over those months (83.56(5)(a)). Whether it also changes your rent going forward is not settled.

If you decide to leave instead, the last day to give 30 days' notice for the month ending March 31 is March 1, 2026. For the month ending April 30, it is March 31, 2026.

tool_calls.result:
Loaded rent_increased. Its instructions:

# Rent increased

Rests on 83.46 (rent, tenancies with no set term), 83.43 (what rent is, good faith), 83.57 (ending a tenancy with no set term), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.425 (local rules), 83.56 (unpaid rent, rent paid, notices), 83.60 (if sued), 83.55 and 83.54 (damages, suits), 83.44 and 83.45 (good faith, unfair clauses), 83.48 (attorney fees), 83.51 and 83.491 (trash, a fee in place of a deposit), 83.59 and 83.67 (no lockout), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets all its readings, and you choose none.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- Part II has no section that sets how much notice a rent increase needs, and none that limits how much rent may go up. Say so plainly when asked. Never state a notice period or a cap as the law.
- Local rules: "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." (83.425), and the section supersedes local rules on matters including "fees charged by the landlord; or notice requirements." (83.425). The stored text holds no local rent rule. Never apply one from memory.
- Rent paid through a program (a voucher, public housing): the program's own rules are not stored. Say they may limit this, and that they are outside this tool.
- The increase comes with an offer to renew, or the tenant would rather leave: load lease_ending too.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the rent, the term, any clause on the rent changing, how the lease may be changed, any charges, staying after the end, and how notices go to the landlord. Quote each clause and cite it.

- **Rent steps set in the lease from the start** (so much until a date, then more): that is the lease's rent, not an increase. Say so.
- **A clause letting the landlord raise the rent during the term:** set the increase beside the clause's conditions (how much notice, how it is given, how much, how often). If it gives a number of days N: the last day to give notice for the start date named is count_days(new_rent_starts, -N), and the earliest start from the notice given is count_days(increase_delivered, N). All conditions met: the rent goes up as the lease says; say so plainly. Any not met: the clause does not support this increase on these terms; say so plainly and go to option 1. A clause with no limit at all: say what it says, that it carries "an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement." (83.44), and that whether it is unfair enough to be "unconscionable" (83.45(1)) is for a court.
- **A new charge** (an amenity fee, a trash fee): the same questions as for rent. The lease provides it: owed as the lease says. It does not: during a set term the landlord cannot add it alone, any more than it can raise the rent. A fee counts as rent only if it is "designated as rent in a written rental agreement." (83.43(12)). That matters because a demand under 83.56(3) and the registry under 83.60(2) speak of rent.
  - Trash: in a unit other than a single-family home or duplex, "Garbage removal and outside receptacles therefor." (83.51(2)(a)) falls to the landlord "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)), though the rental agreement may put the charges on the tenant (83.51(2)(e)).
  - A fee in place of a security deposit: "The amount of the fee, which may not be increased during the term of the rental agreement." (83.491(4)(a)).

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- new_rent: the new amount. increase_delivered: the date word of it reached them, and how it came (handed over, mail, portal, text, spoken). new_rent_starts: the date it is said to start.
- lease_end_date: the date the lease ends, if it has one. period_end: the last day of the rent period before the new rent starts. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- agreed: whether they signed anything or said yes. paid_new_rent: whether they have paid the new amount, for which months, and what they knew about the lease when they paid.
- complaint_date: the date of any complaint before the increase, and what it was. others_rent: what they know about other tenants' rent.
- rent_demand: any written demand for rent, and its date. eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served.

## Which kind of increase

Settle this first. With a set end date, call count_days(lease_end_date, 0) and set new_rent_starts beside the date it gives.

- A set end date, and the new rent starts on or before it: option 1.
- A set end date, and the new rent starts after it: option 2.
- No set end date, or the tenant stayed on after a set term with the landlord's permission: option 3. With no term stated, "the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). Stayed on without permission, or in doubt: load lease_ending too.

Any kind: option 4 if the tenant complained first, and the two parts after it if they fit.

## Option 1: during a set term

Part II has no section that lets a landlord raise the rent during a set term. The rent is what the lease says. Quote the rent clause and any clause on changing the lease.

1. **No clause allows it** (see "What the lease adds").
2. **The tenant did not agree.**
   - They signed a change: the rent is what they signed, if it meets the lease's clause on changes.
   - They said yes without signing: not settled whether that changes the rent. One: a rental agreement can include an "oral agreement for a duration of less than 1 year" (83.43(13)). The other: a lease clause requiring a signed change still governs.
   - They paid it without signing: see "If the tenant already paid it".

Both met: the landlord cannot change the rent alone before the lease ends. Say so plainly. The tenant keeps paying the lease's rent, in full and on time, and can tell the landlord in writing that they do not agree, quoting the rent clause and sending it the way the lease's notice clause says. It helps to keep the letter, the lease, and proof of each payment. Say the risk too: see "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent". The landlord can ask for more when the term ends (option 2).

## Option 2: a higher rent for a new term

Part II names no right to renew at the same rent and no limit on what a landlord may ask for a new term. Say so plainly. The lease's rent stands through lease_end_date whatever the offer says. From there:

- **Agree:** the new rent starts with the new term. Say what they should read before signing: the rent, the term, and any new charge.
- **Leave at the end:** load lease_ending for any notice the lease asks for.
- **Stay without agreeing:** load lease_ending. Staying without permission can mean "double the amount of rent due" (83.58). Read the lease's clause on staying after the end; if it makes the tenancy month to month, say what it says, and option 3 applies from then.

## Option 3: no set end date

Part II sets no notice for this and does not say a landlord may change the rent alone, so what an increase takes is not settled. Give all three readings and choose none. Quote any lease clause on signed changes.

- One: a landlord that can end the tenancy only on 83.57's notice can change the rent only with the same notice, written and delivered a way 83.56(4) names, for month to month "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)).
- Two: no section sets a notice, so none in particular is needed, and the tenant can pay it or leave.
- Three: 83.57 only lets a party end the tenancy, so the rent changes only if the tenant agrees, and a landlord that wants more must end the tenancy on that notice and offer new terms. A lease clause requiring a signed change points this way.

The date: count_days(period_end, -N), with N from 83.57: 30 for month to month (83.57(3)), and for other rent periods the number in 83.57(1), (2), or (4). Set increase_delivered beside it. The ways 83.56(4) names are mailing, a true copy by hand, e-mail under the signed addendum in 83.505(1), or, if the tenant is away, a copy left at the home.

- In writing, a way named, and on or before that date: in time under readings one and two. Say so plainly. Under reading three the letter alone still does not change the rent.
- Later than that, or spoken, or by text or portal: not good for that date under reading one, enough under reading two, and no change under reading three. Whether a late notice works for the next period under reading one is not settled, as lease_ending says of a late notice to end a tenancy; its date is count_days(next_period_end, -N).

Under every reading the landlord may end the tenancy on that notice: it "may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57), and no reason is named. Say so, so the tenant knows what refusing can lead to.

The tenant's choices:

- Pay the new rent. See "If the tenant already paid it" for what paying may mean.
- Pay the old rent and say in writing why. See "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent".
- End the tenancy: load lease_ending. The last day to give notice is count_days(period_end, -N), or count_days(next_period_end, -N) if that has passed.

## Option 4: retaliation

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)).

All of these must be met.

1. **Something the tenant did first.** "Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where:" (83.64(1)) they complained to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), took part in a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), complained to the landlord under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), ended a lease as a servicemember (83.64(1)(d)), paid rent to an association after its demand (83.64(1)(e)), or used fair housing rights (83.64(1)(f)). Fair housing law itself is outside this tool. Another step, like an ordinary repair request: not settled. One: the list is only examples, so it can count. The other: it counts only if it is like the named ones, and a request that says nothing about ending the lease is not 83.56(1)'s complaint.
2. **Good faith.** "In order for the tenant to raise the defense of retaliatory conduct, the tenant must have acted in good faith." (83.64(1)). "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). Applying that is for a court.
3. **Treated differently.** "“Discrimination” under this section means that a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)). Set what they know of other tenants' rent beside the words. The same increase for everyone points against it; say so plainly. If they do not know, say that is the fact to find out.
4. **Primarily because of the complaint.** This is the landlord's motive, for a court. An increase that followed a complaint is not retaliation for that reason alone. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

What it gives: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)), unless "the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)). So not paying the new rent can weaken it; say so.

What the tenant can do about an increase alone, before any case: not settled. One: 83.64(2) makes it only a defense, so there is nothing to raise until a case. The other: 83.64(1) makes the increase unlawful, "Any right or duty declared in this part is enforceable by civil action." (83.54), and a party may recover damages for a failure to comply with "this part" (83.55).

## If the tenant already paid it

"if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).

Ask what they knew when they paid, and set it beside "actual knowledge" (83.56(5)(a)). Whether paying a raised rent gives up the extra, or changes the rent from then on, is not settled. One: paying with knowledge gives up a suit over those months and may show the tenant agreed. The other: an increase the lease never allowed is not rent "due" (83.43(12)), a clause requiring a signed change still stands, and the extra can be claimed under 83.55, with each later month a "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool; do not total them.

## If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent

- **A written demand.** "If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(3)). This tool does not count those days; the demand states them. Say not to ignore it.
- **Taking the old rent.** A landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). So taking it does not mean the landlord gave in. "If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must:" (83.56(5)(a)) give a receipt with the date, the amount, and the balance before filing; or put the amount in the court's registry on filing; or post a new 3-day notice (83.56(5)(a)). Whether the lease's rent is "partial" at all is the dispute.
- **No court case, no removal.** "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)).
- **A case filed.** Say this first. The tenant must pay into the registry "the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon." (83.60(2)). When the amount is what they dispute, the motion is the way to say so: "If a motion to determine rent is filed, documentation in support of the allegation that the rent as alleged in the complaint is in error is required." (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits "only that portion of the full rent for which they are responsible" (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)).
- **Defenses.** The tenant "may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable, that he or she may have, including the defense of retaliatory conduct in accordance with s. 83.64" (83.60(1)(a)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating a notice period or a cap for rent increases as the law.
- Saying a landlord may raise the rent during a set term with no clause and no agreement, or calling the lease's own rent steps an increase.
- Treating 83.57's 30 days as settled for an increase, saying flatly that no notice is needed, or saying flatly that a letter alone changes the rent with no set end date.
- Saying an increase is retaliation because it followed a complaint, or leaving out good faith or being treated differently.
- Telling a tenant they can stop paying rent altogether, explaining a case without 83.60(2), or giving a calendar date for its 5 days.
- Applying a local rent rule from memory.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

### Can the landlord raise the rent in the middle of the lease?
- Your lease says "Rent is $1,050.00 per month, due on the first day of each month" (lease §4). The term runs from August 1, 2025 to July 31, 2026 (lease §3).
- The new rent is to start March 1, 2026. That falls inside the lease term, which ends July 31, 2026.
- Part II of the statute has no section that lets a landlord raise rent during a fixed lease term. It also has no section that caps rent increases or sets a notice period for them.
- Your lease has no clause that lets the landlord raise the rent during the term.
- The lease says it "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant" (lease §10). You told me you signed nothing and didn't agree. So the $1,200 isn't part of your lease.
- The landlord can ask for a higher rent for a new term after July 31, 2026. Your lease says that if you stay after that date with the landlord's written consent, the tenancy becomes month to month "on the same terms" (lease §9).

### What should you do now?
- Keep paying $1,050, in full and on time. Keep proof of each payment.
- Send your landlord a short written note saying you don't agree and that your lease sets rent at $1,050 through July 31, 2026. Quote lease §4 and §10.
- Lease §7 says to deliver written notices to the landlord by hand at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or by certified mail to that address. Keep a copy of the letter, the lease, and the landlord's letter.

### What is the risk of paying only $1,050?
- Your landlord might treat the $150 difference as unpaid rent. Under 83.56(3), if rent isn't paid when due and the default continues for 3 days (excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays) after a written demand, the landlord "may terminate the rental agreement."
- If you get a written demand, don't ignore it. Your position would be that the lease rent is the only rent due.
- A landlord can't remove you without a court case, except if you give up or abandon the home (83.59(3)). A landlord also can't block your access to the home (83.67(2)).
- If a case is filed, you would have to pay rent into the court registry or file a motion to determine rent within 5 days (excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays) after being served (83.60(2)). Missing that can waive your defenses.
- If the landlord accepts $1,050, that doesn't give up the landlord's right to claim more (83.56(5)(a)).

### What would change this answer?
- Rent paid through a program: that program's own rules might limit what you pay. Those rules are outside this tool.
- Signing or agreeing: if you sign a change, the rent becomes what you signed. Saying yes without signing is not settled. One reading is that an oral agreement can count (83.43(13)). The other is that the lease's signed-writing clause still controls (lease §10).
- Paying $1,200: if you pay the higher rent knowing the lease says $1,050, you may give up a claim for those months (83.56(5)(a)). Whether that also changes your rent going forward is not settled.

# Rent increased

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- Part II has no section that sets how much notice a rent increase needs, and none that limits how much rent may go up. Say so plainly when asked. Never state a notice period or a cap as the law.

(83.425), and the section supersedes local rules on matters including "fees charged by the landlord; or notice requirements." (83.425). The stored text holds no local rent rule. Never apply one from memory.
