answer:
It's not settled whether a landlord can raise your rent with this little notice. Florida's landlord-tenant law sets no notice period for a rent increase and no cap on how much rent can go up. It does set 30 days' notice to end a month-to-month tenancy, and courts could apply that to an increase. If they do, your letter was too late for April. You haven't agreed and you haven't paid the new rent. Your lease has a clause requiring signed changes, which helps you.

What you can do:
- Keep paying $1,050, on time and in full.
- Tell your landlord in writing that you don't agree.
- Keep copies of everything.
- Know that your landlord can end a month-to-month tenancy with proper written notice, for any reason. That risk applies whichever reading is right.

Did you complain to the landlord, or to a city or county code office, about anything before this letter came?

DETAILS

### Does Florida law set a notice period or a cap for rent increases?
No. Part II of the statute has no section on how much notice an increase needs, and none that limits how much rent can go up. Local rules can't fill that gap. The statute says these matters are "preempted to the state" (83.425). I haven't applied any local rule.

### What does your lease say?
- Rent is "$1,050.00 per month" (¶4). The lease has no clause letting the landlord raise the rent.
- The tenancy "continues from month to month until ended by Tenant or Landlord" (¶3).
- The lease "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant" (¶10).
- Notices to you "shall be delivered to the apartment while Tenant lives there" (¶8). A letter handed to you at your door fits that.

### Was the letter in time? Three readings, and I'm choosing none
This is your situation. Your tenancy has no end date. The letter was handed to you on March 20. The new rent is said to start April 1. The last rent period before that ends March 31.

1. **The 30-day rule applies to increases.**
   - Ending a month-to-month tenancy takes "not less than 30 days' notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)). The notice must be written and delivered one of the ways in 83.56(4). Hand delivery of a true copy is one of them.
   - Counting back 30 days from March 31 gives March 1. That date has passed, so the letter was too late for April.
   - If the same notice rule applies to the next period, which ends April 30, the last day for notice is March 31. That date has not passed. Whether a late notice carries over to the next period is not settled.
2. **No notice is required.** No section sets one, so the letter could be enough. You would then pay the new rent or leave.
3. **Only your agreement changes the rent.** Section 83.57 only lets a party end the tenancy. It doesn't let a landlord change the rent alone. A landlord who wants more would have to end the tenancy and offer new terms. Your lease's signed-change clause (¶10) points this way.

### Can your landlord end your tenancy instead?
Yes, under every reading. A month-to-month tenancy "may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57). The statute names no required reason.

### What happens if you keep paying $1,050?
- Your landlord may treat the $150 difference as unpaid rent and send a written demand. The demand gives you "3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays" to pay or leave (83.56(3)). Don't ignore a demand like that.
- Accepting the lower amount doesn't mean the landlord gave in. A landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period" (83.56(5)(a)). Whether $1,050 counts as "partial" rent is the exact point in dispute.
- If a court case is filed, you must pay rent into the court registry, or file a motion about the amount, within 5 days (not counting weekends and legal holidays) of being served. Missing that waives your defenses other than payment (83.60(2)).
- The landlord can't remove you or lock you out without a court case (83.59(3), 83.67(2)).

### If you pay the new rent, what does that mean?
Paying with "actual knowledge" of a problem can give up your right to sue over it (83.56(5)(a)). It may also be treated as agreeing to the new rent. That is not settled. Since you haven't paid it, this is a reason to think before you do.

### Could this be retaliation?
Raising rent is unlawful if it is "primarily because the landlord is retaliating" (83.64(1)). Three things must be true:
- You did something protected first, such as complaining to a code agency or to the landlord about a repair (83.64(1)(a), (c)).
- You acted in good faith.
- You were treated differently from other tenants (83.64(4)).

If everyone got the same increase, that points against retaliation. If you complained before this letter, tell me what and when.

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- new_rent: the new amount. increase_delivered: the date word of it reached them, and how it came (handed over, mail, portal, text, spoken). new_rent_starts: the date it is said to start.
- lease_end_date: the date the lease ends, if it has one. period_end: the last day of the rent period before the new rent starts. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- agreed: whether they signed anything or said yes. paid_new_rent: whether they have paid the new amount, for which months, and what they knew about the lease when they paid.
- complaint_date: the date of any complaint before the increase, and what it was. others_rent: what they know about other tenants' rent.
- rent_demand: any written demand for rent, and its date. eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served.

## Which kind of increase

Settle this first. With a set end date, call count_days(lease_end_date, 0) and set new_rent_starts beside the date it gives.

- A set end date, and the new rent starts on or before it: option 1.
- A set end date, and the new rent starts after it: option 2.
- No set end date, or the tenant stayed on after a set term with the landlord's permission: option 3. With no term stated, "the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). Stayed on without permission, or in doubt: load lease_ending too.

Any kind: option 4 if the tenant complained first, and the two parts after it if they fit.

## Option 1: during a set term

Part II has no section that lets a landlord raise the rent during a set term. The rent is what the lease says. Quote the rent clause and any clause on changing the lease.

1. **No clause allows it** (see "What the lease adds").
2. **The tenant did not agree.**
   - They signed a change: the rent is what they signed, if it meets the lease's clause on changes.
   - They said yes without signing: not settled whether that changes the rent. One: a rental agreement can include an "oral agreement for a duration of less than 1 year" (83.43(13)). The other: a lease clause requiring a signed change still governs.
   - They paid it without signing: see "If the tenant already paid it".

Both met: the landlord cannot change the rent alone before the lease ends. Say so plainly. The tenant keeps paying the lease's rent, in full and on time, and can tell the landlord in writing that they do not agree, quoting the rent clause and sending it the way the lease's notice clause says. It helps to keep the letter, the lease, and proof of each payment. Say the risk too: see "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent". The landlord can ask for more when the term ends (option 2).

## Option 2: a higher rent for a new term

Part II names no right to renew at the same rent and no limit on what a landlord may ask for a new term. Say so plainly. The lease's rent stands through lease_end_date whatever the offer says. From there:

- **Agree:** the new rent starts with the new term. Say what they should read before signing: the rent, the term, and any new charge.
- **Leave at the end:** load lease_ending for any notice the lease asks for.
- **Stay without agreeing:** load lease_ending. Staying without permission can mean "double the amount of rent due" (83.58). Read the lease's clause on staying after the end; if it makes the tenancy month to month, say what it says, and option 3 applies from then.

## Option 3: no set end date

Part II sets no notice for this and does not say a landlord may change the rent alone, so what an increase takes is not settled. Give all three readings and choose none. Quote any lease clause on signed changes.

- One: a landlord that can end the tenancy only on 83.57's notice can change the rent only with the same notice, written and delivered a way 83.56(4) names, for month to month "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)).
- Two: no section sets a notice, so none in particular is needed, and the tenant can pay it or leave.
- Three: 83.57 only lets a party end the tenancy, so the rent changes only if the tenant agrees, and a landlord that wants more must end the tenancy on that notice and offer new terms. A lease clause requiring a signed change points this way.

The date: count_days(period_end, -N), with N from 83.57: 30 for month to month (83.57(3)), and for other rent periods the number in 83.57(1), (2), or (4). Set increase_delivered beside it. The ways 83.56(4) names are mailing, a true copy by hand, e-mail under the signed addendum in 83.505(1), or, if the tenant is away, a copy left at the home.

- In writing, a way named, and on or before that date: in time under readings one and two. Say so plainly. Under reading three the letter alone still does not change the rent.
- Later than that, or spoken, or by text or portal: not good for that date under reading one, enough under reading two, and no change under reading three. Whether a late notice works for the next period under reading one is not settled, as lease_ending says of a late notice to end a tenancy; its date is count_days(next_period_end, -N).

Under every reading the landlord may end the tenancy on that notice: it "may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57), and no reason is named. Say so, so the tenant knows what refusing can lead to.

The tenant's choices:

- Pay the new rent. See "If the tenant already paid it" for what paying may mean.
- Pay the old rent and say in writing why. See "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent".
- End the tenancy: load lease_ending. The last day to give notice is count_days(period_end, -N), or count_days(next_period_end, -N) if that has passed.

## Option 4: retaliation

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)).

All of these must be met.

1. **Something the tenant did first.** "Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where:" (83.64(1)) they complained to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), took part in a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), complained to the landlord under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), ended a lease as a servicemember (83.64(1)(d)), paid rent to an association after its demand (83.64(1)(e)), or used fair housing rights (83.64(1)(f)). Fair housing law itself is outside this tool. Another step, like an ordinary repair request: not settled. One: the list is only examples, so it can count. The other: it counts only if it is like the named ones, and a request that says nothing about ending the lease is not 83.56(1)'s complaint.
2. **Good faith.** "In order for the tenant to raise the defense of retaliatory conduct, the tenant must have acted in good faith." (83.64(1)). "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). Applying that is for a court.
3. **Treated differently.** "“Discrimination” under this section means that a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)). Set what they know of other tenants' rent beside the words. The same increase for everyone points against it; say so plainly. If they do not know, say that is the fact to find out.
4. **Primarily because of the complaint.** This is the landlord's motive, for a court. An increase that followed a complaint is not retaliation for that reason alone. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

What it gives: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)), unless "the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)). So not paying the new rent can weaken it; say so.

What the tenant can do about an increase alone, before any case: not settled. One: 83.64(2) makes it only a defense, so there is nothing to raise until a case. The other: 83.64(1) makes the increase unlawful, "Any right or duty declared in this part is enforceable by civil action." (83.54), and a party may recover damages for a failure to comply with "this part" (83.55).

## If the tenant already paid it

"if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).

Ask what they knew when they paid, and set it beside "actual knowledge" (83.56(5)(a)). Whether paying a raised rent gives up the extra, or changes the rent from then on, is not settled. One: paying with knowledge gives up a suit over those months and may show the tenant agreed. The other: an increase the lease never allowed is not rent "due" (83.43(12)), a clause requiring a signed change still stands, and the extra can be claimed under 83.55, with each later month a "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool; do not total them.

## If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent

- **A written demand.** "If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(3)). This tool does not count those days; the demand states them. Say not to ignore it.
- **Taking the old rent.** A landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). So taking it does not mean the landlord gave in. "If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must:" (83.56(5)(a)) give a receipt with the date, the amount, and the balance before filing; or put the amount in the court's registry on filing; or post a new 3-day notice (83.56(5)(a)). Whether the lease's rent is "partial" at all is the dispute.
- **No court case, no removal.** "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)).
- **A case filed.** Say this first. The tenant must pay into the registry "the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon." (83.60(2)). When the amount is what they dispute, the motion is the way to say so: "If a motion to determine rent is filed, documentation in support of the allegation that the rent as alleged in the complaint is in error is required." (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits "only that portion of the full rent for which they are responsible" (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)).
- **Defenses.** The tenant "may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable, that he or she may have, including the defense of retaliatory conduct in accordance with s. 83.64" (83.60(1)(a)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating a notice period or a cap for rent increases as the law.
- Saying a landlord may raise the rent during a set term with no clause and no agreement, or calling the lease's own rent steps an increase.
- Treating 83.57's 30 days as settled for an increase, saying flatly that no notice is needed, or saying flatly that a letter alone changes the rent with no set end date.
- Saying an increase is retaliation because it followed a complaint, or leaving out good faith or being treated differently.
- Telling a tenant they can stop paying rent altogether, explaining a case without 83.60(2), or giving a calendar date for its 5 days.
- Applying a local rent rule from memory.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

DETAILS

### Can the landlord raise the rent during your lease?
- Your lease runs from August 1, 2025 to July 31, 2026 (lease §3). The new rent was to start March 1, 2026, which is inside that term.
- Lease §4 says: "Rent is $1,050.00 per month." Lease §10 says the lease "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant."
- Nothing in the lease lets the landlord raise the rent during the term. The lease has no rent-increase clause.
- Florida's landlord-tenant law (Part II) has no section that lets a landlord raise rent during a set term. It also has no section that caps increases or sets a notice period for them.
- You told me you signed nothing and only started paying the new amount. So on this record, the rent under the lease stays $1,050 until July 31, 2026.
- The landlord can ask for more rent for a new term after July 31. That is a separate question.

### Did paying $1,150 change your rent?
This is not settled. There are two readings.
- **Paying counts as agreeing.** Part II says a rental agreement can include an "oral agreement for a duration of less than 1 year" (83.43(13)). Paying the higher amount without objection could be read as accepting it.
- **Paying doesn't change the rent.** Lease §10 requires a signed writing. An increase the lease never allowed is arguably not rent "due" (83.43(12)). On this reading, each month is a new question.

### Can you get the extra $100 for March and April back?
This is also not settled.
- Section 83.56(5)(a) says that if a tenant "pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord," the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance."
- You knew the amount was higher when you paid, but you hadn't read the lease. Whether that is "actual knowledge" of a noncompliance is for a court.
- **Reading one:** paying with that knowledge gave up a claim for those two months. It may also show you agreed to the new rent.
- **Reading two:** the extra can still be claimed as damages for failure to follow Part II (83.55). Each later month would be a "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" that you did not waive.
- I can't say how a court would decide, and I won't total any amounts.

### What are the risks of paying $1,050 now?
- The landlord may say you underpaid and send a written demand. Under 83.56(3), if rent isn't paid and "the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand," the landlord "may terminate the rental agreement."
- Whether $1,050 is "partial rent" or the full rent is the real dispute. Under 83.56(5)(a), a landlord that accepts partial rent does not give up its right to act on the shortfall.
- A landlord can't remove you without a court case (83.59(3)) and can't lock you out (83.67(2)).
- If a case is filed, you must pay rent into the court registry or file a motion about the amount within 5 days (excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays) after you are served (83.60(2)). If you don't, you lose your defenses except payment, and the landlord can get an immediate default judgment for removal.

### What can you do to protect yourself?
- Pay $1,050 in full and on time, and keep proof of each payment.
- Send the landlord a written notice that you don't agree to the increase. Quote lease §4 and §10.
- Lease §7 says to deliver that notice by hand to 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send it there by certified mail. Keep a copy.
- Keep your lease and your payment records for March and April.

tool_calls.result:
Loaded rent_increased. Its instructions:

# Rent increased

Rests on 83.46 (rent, tenancies with no set term), 83.43 (what rent is, good faith), 83.57 (ending a tenancy with no set term), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.425 (local rules), 83.56 (unpaid rent, rent paid, notices), 83.60 (if sued), 83.55 and 83.54 (damages, suits), 83.44 and 83.45 (good faith, unfair clauses), 83.48 (attorney fees), 83.51 and 83.491 (trash, a fee in place of a deposit), 83.59 and 83.67 (no lockout), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets all its readings, and you choose none.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- Part II has no section that sets how much notice a rent increase needs, and none that limits how much rent may go up. Say so plainly when asked. Never state a notice period or a cap as the law.
- Local rules: "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." (83.425), and the section supersedes local rules on matters including "fees charged by the landlord; or notice requirements." (83.425). The stored text holds no local rent rule. Never apply one from memory.
- Rent paid through a program (a voucher, public housing): the program's own rules are not stored. Say they may limit this, and that they are outside this tool.
- The increase comes with an offer to renew, or the tenant would rather leave: load lease_ending too.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the rent, the term, any clause on the rent changing, how the lease may be changed, any charges, staying after the end, and how notices go to the landlord. Quote each clause and cite it.

- **Rent steps set in the lease from the start** (so much until a date, then more): that is the lease's rent, not an increase. Say so.
- **A clause letting the landlord raise the rent during the term:** set the increase beside the clause's conditions (how much notice, how it is given, how much, how often). If it gives a number of days N: the last day to give notice for the start date named is count_days(new_rent_starts, -N), and the earliest start from the notice given is count_days(increase_delivered, N). All conditions met: the rent goes up as the lease says; say so plainly. Any not met: the clause does not support this increase on these terms; say so plainly and go to option 1. A clause with no limit at all: say what it says, that it carries "an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement." (83.44), and that whether it is unfair enough to be "unconscionable" (83.45(1)) is for a court.
- **A new charge** (an amenity fee, a trash fee): the same questions as for rent. The lease provides it: owed as the lease says. It does not: during a set term the landlord cannot add it alone, any more than it can raise the rent. A fee counts as rent only if it is "designated as rent in a written rental agreement." (83.43(12)). That matters because a demand under 83.56(3) and the registry under 83.60(2) speak of rent.
  - Trash: in a unit other than a single-family home or duplex, "Garbage removal and outside receptacles therefor." (83.51(2)(a)) falls to the landlord "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)), though the rental agreement may put the charges on the tenant (83.51(2)(e)).
  - A fee in place of a security deposit: "The amount of the fee, which may not be increased during the term of the rental agreement." (83.491(4)(a)).

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- new_rent: the new amount. increase_delivered: the date word of it reached them, and how it came (handed over, mail, portal, text, spoken). new_rent_starts: the date it is said to start.
- lease_end_date: the date the lease ends, if it has one. period_end: the last day of the rent period before the new rent starts. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- agreed: whether they signed anything or said yes. paid_new_rent: whether they have paid the new amount, for which months, and what they knew about the lease when they paid.
- complaint_date: the date of any complaint before the increase, and what it was. others_rent: what they know about other tenants' rent.
- rent_demand: any written demand for rent, and its date. eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served.

## Which kind of increase

Settle this first. With a set end date, call count_days(lease_end_date, 0) and set new_rent_starts beside the date it gives.

- A set end date, and the new rent starts on or before it: option 1.
- A set end date, and the new rent starts after it: option 2.
- No set end date, or the tenant stayed on after a set term with the landlord's permission: option 3. With no term stated, "the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). Stayed on without permission, or in doubt: load lease_ending too.

Any kind: option 4 if the tenant complained first, and the two parts after it if they fit.

## Option 1: during a set term

Part II has no section that lets a landlord raise the rent during a set term. The rent is what the lease says. Quote the rent clause and any clause on changing the lease.

1. **No clause allows it** (see "What the lease adds").
2. **The tenant did not agree.**
   - They signed a change: the rent is what they signed, if it meets the lease's clause on changes.
   - They said yes without signing: not settled whether that changes the rent. One: a rental agreement can include an "oral agreement for a duration of less than 1 year" (83.43(13)). The other: a lease clause requiring a signed change still governs.
   - They paid it without signing: see "If the tenant already paid it".

Both met: the landlord cannot change the rent alone before the lease ends. Say so plainly. The tenant keeps paying the lease's rent, in full and on time, and can tell the landlord in writing that they do not agree, quoting the rent clause and sending it the way the lease's notice clause says. It helps to keep the letter, the lease, and proof of each payment. Say the risk too: see "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent". The landlord can ask for more when the term ends (option 2).

## Option 2: a higher rent for a new term

Part II names no right to renew at the same rent and no limit on what a landlord may ask for a new term. Say so plainly. The lease's rent stands through lease_end_date whatever the offer says. From there:

- **Agree:** the new rent starts with the new term. Say what they should read before signing: the rent, the term, and any new charge.
- **Leave at the end:** load lease_ending for any notice the lease asks for.
- **Stay without agreeing:** load lease_ending. Staying without permission can mean "double the amount of rent due" (83.58). Read the lease's clause on staying after the end; if it makes the tenancy month to month, say what it says, and option 3 applies from then.

## Option 3: no set end date

Part II sets no notice for this and does not say a landlord may change the rent alone, so what an increase takes is not settled. Give all three readings and choose none. Quote any lease clause on signed changes.

- One: a landlord that can end the tenancy only on 83.57's notice can change the rent only with the same notice, written and delivered a way 83.56(4) names, for month to month "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)).
- Two: no section sets a notice, so none in particular is needed, and the tenant can pay it or leave.
- Three: 83.57 only lets a party end the tenancy, so the rent changes only if the tenant agrees, and a landlord that wants more must end the tenancy on that notice and offer new terms. A lease clause requiring a signed change points this way.

The date: count_days(period_end, -N), with N from 83.57: 30 for month to month (83.57(3)), and for other rent periods the number in 83.57(1), (2), or (4). Set increase_delivered beside it. The ways 83.56(4) names are mailing, a true copy by hand, e-mail under the signed addendum in 83.505(1), or, if the tenant is away, a copy left at the home.

- In writing, a way named, and on or before that date: in time under readings one and two. Say so plainly. Under reading three the letter alone still does not change the rent.
- Later than that, or spoken, or by text or portal: not good for that date under reading one, enough under reading two, and no change under reading three. Whether a late notice works for the next period under reading one is not settled, as lease_ending says of a late notice to end a tenancy; its date is count_days(next_period_end, -N).

Under every reading the landlord may end the tenancy on that notice: it "may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57), and no reason is named. Say so, so the tenant knows what refusing can lead to.

The tenant's choices:

- Pay the new rent. See "If the tenant already paid it" for what paying may mean.
- Pay the old rent and say in writing why. See "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent".
- End the tenancy: load lease_ending. The last day to give notice is count_days(period_end, -N), or count_days(next_period_end, -N) if that has passed.

## Option 4: retaliation

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)).

All of these must be met.

1. **Something the tenant did first.** "Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where:" (83.64(1)) they complained to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), took part in a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), complained to the landlord under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), ended a lease as a servicemember (83.64(1)(d)), paid rent to an association after its demand (83.64(1)(e)), or used fair housing rights (83.64(1)(f)). Fair housing law itself is outside this tool. Another step, like an ordinary repair request: not settled. One: the list is only examples, so it can count. The other: it counts only if it is like the named ones, and a request that says nothing about ending the lease is not 83.56(1)'s complaint.
2. **Good faith.** "In order for the tenant to raise the defense of retaliatory conduct, the tenant must have acted in good faith." (83.64(1)). "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). Applying that is for a court.
3. **Treated differently.** "“Discrimination” under this section means that a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)). Set what they know of other tenants' rent beside the words. The same increase for everyone points against it; say so plainly. If they do not know, say that is the fact to find out.
4. **Primarily because of the complaint.** This is the landlord's motive, for a court. An increase that followed a complaint is not retaliation for that reason alone. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

What it gives: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)), unless "the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)). So not paying the new rent can weaken it; say so.

What the tenant can do about an increase alone, before any case: not settled. One: 83.64(2) makes it only a defense, so there is nothing to raise until a case. The other: 83.64(1) makes the increase unlawful, "Any right or duty declared in this part is enforceable by civil action." (83.54), and a party may recover damages for a failure to comply with "this part" (83.55).

## If the tenant already paid it

"if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).

Ask what they knew when they paid, and set it beside "actual knowledge" (83.56(5)(a)). Whether paying a raised rent gives up the extra, or changes the rent from then on, is not settled. One: paying with knowledge gives up a suit over those months and may show the tenant agreed. The other: an increase the lease never allowed is not rent "due" (83.43(12)), a clause requiring a signed change still stands, and the extra can be claimed under 83.55, with each later month a "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool; do not total them.

## If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent

- **A written demand.** "If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(3)). This tool does not count those days; the demand states them. Say not to ignore it.
- **Taking the old rent.** A landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). So taking it does not mean the landlord gave in. "If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must:" (83.56(5)(a)) give a receipt with the date, the amount, and the balance before filing; or put the amount in the court's registry on filing; or post a new 3-day notice (83.56(5)(a)). Whether the lease's rent is "partial" at all is the dispute.
- **No court case, no removal.** "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)).
- **A case filed.** Say this first. The tenant must pay into the registry "the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon." (83.60(2)). When the amount is what they dispute, the motion is the way to say so: "If a motion to determine rent is filed, documentation in support of the allegation that the rent as alleged in the complaint is in error is required." (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits "only that portion of the full rent for which they are responsible" (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)).
- **Defenses.** The tenant "may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable, that he or she may have, including the defense of retaliatory conduct in accordance with s. 83.64" (83.60(1)(a)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating a notice period or a cap for rent increases as the law.
- Saying a landlord may raise the rent during a set term with no clause and no agreement, or calling the lease's own rent steps an increase.
- Treating 83.57's 30 days as settled for an increase, saying flatly that no notice is needed, or saying flatly that a letter alone changes the rent with no set end date.
- Saying an increase is retaliation because it followed a complaint, or leaving out good faith or being treated differently.
- Telling a tenant they can stop paying rent altogether, explaining a case without 83.60(2), or giving a calendar date for its 5 days.
- Applying a local rent rule from memory.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

tool_calls.result: 83.56 Termination of rental agreement. — (1) If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement. If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable. (b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance. (2) If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may: (a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of such noncompliance include, but are not limited to, activities in contravention of the lease or this part such as having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary. If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that (cite the noncompliance) . Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice or your lease shall be deemed terminated and you shall vacate the premises upon such termination. If this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months, your tenancy is subject to termination without further warning and without your being given an opportunity to cure the noncompliance. (3) If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. Legal holidays for the purpose of this section shall be court-observed holidays only. The 3-day notice shall contain a statement in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that you are indebted to me in the sum of dollars for the rent and use of the premises (address of leased premises, including county) , Florida, now occupied by you and that I demand payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days (excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays) from the date of delivery of this notice, to wit: on or before the day of , (year) . (landlord’s name, address and phone number) (4) The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence. The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement. (5)(a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must: 1. Provide the tenant with a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed-upon date and balance of rent due before filing an action for possession; 2. Place the amount of partial rent accepted from the tenant in the registry of the court upon filing the action for possession; or 3. Post a new 3-day notice reflecting the new amount due. (b) Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2). The court may not set a date for mediation or trial unless the provisions of s. 83.60 (2) have been met, but must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately if the tenant fails to comply with s. 83.60 (2). (c) This subsection does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government or an agency of local, state, or national government; however, waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance. (6) If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3). answer:
**Short answer:** It's not settled whether your landlord can raise the rent on its own in a month-to-month tenancy. Florida's landlord-tenant law sets no cap on increases and no notice period for them. Retaliation looks unlikely on your facts, mainly because every unit got the same increase. Your landlord also gave you written notice, handed to you at your door, before the date it was due. Under two of the three readings below, that notice is enough to raise your rent to $1,102.50 from April 1. Under the third, the letter alone doesn't change your rent unless you agree.

Does your portal repair request say anything about ending your lease if the faucet isn't fixed?

DETAILS

### Does Florida law limit or set notice for a rent increase?
Part II has no section that caps how much rent can go up. It also has none that says how much notice an increase needs. Local rules can't fill the gap, because "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." (83.425).

### Can the landlord change the rent without your agreement?
Your lease is month to month (lease §3), so it has no set end date. Part II doesn't say how a landlord changes rent in that situation, so there are three readings. I'm not choosing one.
- **Reading one:** An increase needs the same notice as ending a month-to-month tenancy. That is "not less than 30 days' notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)). It must be written and delivered in a way 83.56(4) names, such as "delivering a true copy thereof."
- **Reading two:** No section sets a notice for increases, so none in particular is needed. You can pay the new rent or leave.
- **Reading three:** Section 83.57 only lets either side end the tenancy. Under this reading, the rent changes only if you agree. A landlord who wants more would have to end the tenancy and offer new terms. Lease §10 points this way: the lease "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant." You told me you did not agree.

Measured against reading one, your landlord's notice was on time:
- Your rent period ends March 31. The last day to give 30 days' notice for that period is March 1, and that date has not passed.
- The letter was handed to you at your door on February 20. That is a hand delivery in writing, and lease §8 says notices go "to the apartment."
- So the notice is in time under readings one and two. Under reading three, the letter alone still doesn't change your rent.

Under any reading, your landlord can end a month-to-month tenancy with written notice, and the law names no reason it must give (83.57). If you refuse the increase, that is a risk.

### Is it retaliation?
Four things must all be true (83.64).
1. **Something you did first.** The law says a landlord can't retaliate when a tenant "has complained to the landlord pursuant to s. 83.56 (1)" (83.64(1)(c)). That kind of complaint is a written notice that names the problem and says you intend to end the lease if it isn't fixed (83.56(1)). The listed examples are only examples (83.64(1)). A plain portal repair request is not settled.
   - One reading is that any good-faith complaint can count, because the list isn't complete.
   - The other is that it must be like the listed ones. Under that reading, a request that says nothing about ending the lease isn't an 83.56(1) complaint.
   That's why I'm asking what your request said.
2. **Good faith.** You must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)). That means "honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). A court applies that.
3. **Different treatment.** "'Discrimination' under this section means that a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged… which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)). You told me every unit got the same letter and the same percentage. That points against retaliation.
4. **Motive.** The increase must be "primarily because the landlord is retaliating" (83.64(1)). That is for a court. An increase that came after a complaint is not retaliation for that reason alone. You made the request on January 20 and got the letter on February 20.

Retaliation is raised as a defense if your landlord sues to evict you (83.64(2)). It doesn't apply if the landlord proves good cause, and "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" are an example (83.64(3)). Whether you can act on an increase alone, before any case, is also not settled. One reading is that 83.64(2) makes it only a defense. The other is that 83.64(1) makes the increase unlawful and 83.54 and 83.55 let you sue for it.

### What are your choices?
- **Pay the new rent.** If you pay with actual knowledge that your landlord broke the rules, you give up the right to sue over that (83.56(5)(a)). Whether paying also shows you agreed to the new rent is not settled.
- **Pay the old rent and explain in writing.** Your landlord can treat that as unpaid rent and send a written 3-day demand (83.56(3)). Don't ignore a demand. Taking partial rent doesn't waive your landlord's rights (83.56(5)(a)). Not paying the new rent can also weaken a retaliation defense.
- **Leave.** Ending a month-to-month tenancy takes written notice at least 30 days before the end of a monthly period (83.57(3)). Your next period ends April 30. The last day to give that notice for it is March 31.

Under lease §7, any written notice to your landlord must be handed to the office at Suite A or sent there by certified mail.

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded rent_increased. Its instructions:

# Rent increased

Rests on 83.46 (rent, tenancies with no set term), 83.43 (what rent is, good faith), 83.57 (ending a tenancy with no set term), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.425 (local rules), 83.56 (unpaid rent, rent paid, notices), 83.60 (if sued), 83.55 and 83.54 (damages, suits), 83.44 and 83.45 (good faith, unfair clauses), 83.48 (attorney fees), 83.51 and 83.491 (trash, a fee in place of a deposit), 83.59 and 83.67 (no lockout), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets all its readings, and you choose none.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- Part II has no section that sets how much notice a rent increase needs, and none that limits how much rent may go up. Say so plainly when asked. Never state a notice period or a cap as the law.
- Local rules: "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." (83.425), and the section supersedes local rules on matters including "fees charged by the landlord; or notice requirements." (83.425). The stored text holds no local rent rule. Never apply one from memory.
- Rent paid through a program (a voucher, public housing): the program's own rules are not stored. Say they may limit this, and that they are outside this tool.
- The increase comes with an offer to renew, or the tenant would rather leave: load lease_ending too.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the rent, the term, any clause on the rent changing, how the lease may be changed, any charges, staying after the end, and how notices go to the landlord. Quote each clause and cite it.

- **Rent steps set in the lease from the start** (so much until a date, then more): that is the lease's rent, not an increase. Say so.
- **A clause letting the landlord raise the rent during the term:** set the increase beside the clause's conditions (how much notice, how it is given, how much, how often). If it gives a number of days N: the last day to give notice for the start date named is count_days(new_rent_starts, -N), and the earliest start from the notice given is count_days(increase_delivered, N). All conditions met: the rent goes up as the lease says; say so plainly. Any not met: the clause does not support this increase on these terms; say so plainly and go to option 1. A clause with no limit at all: say what it says, that it carries "an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement." (83.44), and that whether it is unfair enough to be "unconscionable" (83.45(1)) is for a court.
- **A new charge** (an amenity fee, a trash fee): the same questions as for rent. The lease provides it: owed as the lease says. It does not: during a set term the landlord cannot add it alone, any more than it can raise the rent. A fee counts as rent only if it is "designated as rent in a written rental agreement." (83.43(12)). That matters because a demand under 83.56(3) and the registry under 83.60(2) speak of rent.
  - Trash: in a unit other than a single-family home or duplex, "Garbage removal and outside receptacles therefor." (83.51(2)(a)) falls to the landlord "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)), though the rental agreement may put the charges on the tenant (83.51(2)(e)).
  - A fee in place of a security deposit: "The amount of the fee, which may not be increased during the term of the rental agreement." (83.491(4)(a)).

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- new_rent: the new amount. increase_delivered: the date word of it reached them, and how it came (handed over, mail, portal, text, spoken). new_rent_starts: the date it is said to start.
- lease_end_date: the date the lease ends, if it has one. period_end: the last day of the rent period before the new rent starts. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- agreed: whether they signed anything or said yes. paid_new_rent: whether they have paid the new amount, for which months, and what they knew about the lease when they paid.
- complaint_date: the date of any complaint before the increase, and what it was. others_rent: what they know about other tenants' rent.
- rent_demand: any written demand for rent, and its date. eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served.

## Which kind of increase

Settle this first. With a set end date, call count_days(lease_end_date, 0) and set new_rent_starts beside the date it gives.

- A set end date, and the new rent starts on or before it: option 1.
- A set end date, and the new rent starts after it: option 2.
- No set end date, or the tenant stayed on after a set term with the landlord's permission: option 3. With no term stated, "the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). Stayed on without permission, or in doubt: load lease_ending too.

Any kind: option 4 if the tenant complained first, and the two parts after it if they fit.

## Option 1: during a set term

Part II has no section that lets a landlord raise the rent during a set term. The rent is what the lease says. Quote the rent clause and any clause on changing the lease.

1. **No clause allows it** (see "What the lease adds").
2. **The tenant did not agree.**
   - They signed a change: the rent is what they signed, if it meets the lease's clause on changes.
   - They said yes without signing: not settled whether that changes the rent. One: a rental agreement can include an "oral agreement for a duration of less than 1 year" (83.43(13)). The other: a lease clause requiring a signed change still governs.
   - They paid it without signing: see "If the tenant already paid it".

Both met: the landlord cannot change the rent alone before the lease ends. Say so plainly. The tenant keeps paying the lease's rent, in full and on time, and can tell the landlord in writing that they do not agree, quoting the rent clause and sending it the way the lease's notice clause says. It helps to keep the letter, the lease, and proof of each payment. Say the risk too: see "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent". The landlord can ask for more when the term ends (option 2).

## Option 2: a higher rent for a new term

Part II names no right to renew at the same rent and no limit on what a landlord may ask for a new term. Say so plainly. The lease's rent stands through lease_end_date whatever the offer says. From there:

- **Agree:** the new rent starts with the new term. Say what they should read before signing: the rent, the term, and any new charge.
- **Leave at the end:** load lease_ending for any notice the lease asks for.
- **Stay without agreeing:** load lease_ending. Staying without permission can mean "double the amount of rent due" (83.58). Read the lease's clause on staying after the end; if it makes the tenancy month to month, say what it says, and option 3 applies from then.

## Option 3: no set end date

Part II sets no notice for this and does not say a landlord may change the rent alone, so what an increase takes is not settled. Give all three readings and choose none. Quote any lease clause on signed changes.

- One: a landlord that can end the tenancy only on 83.57's notice can change the rent only with the same notice, written and delivered a way 83.56(4) names, for month to month "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)).
- Two: no section sets a notice, so none in particular is needed, and the tenant can pay it or leave.
- Three: 83.57 only lets a party end the tenancy, so the rent changes only if the tenant agrees, and a landlord that wants more must end the tenancy on that notice and offer new terms. A lease clause requiring a signed change points this way.

The date: count_days(period_end, -N), with N from 83.57: 30 for month to month (83.57(3)), and for other rent periods the number in 83.57(1), (2), or (4). Set increase_delivered beside it. The ways 83.56(4) names are mailing, a true copy by hand, e-mail under the signed addendum in 83.505(1), or, if the tenant is away, a copy left at the home.

- In writing, a way named, and on or before that date: in time under readings one and two. Say so plainly. Under reading three the letter alone still does not change the rent.
- Later than that, or spoken, or by text or portal: not good for that date under reading one, enough under reading two, and no change under reading three. Whether a late notice works for the next period under reading one is not settled, as lease_ending says of a late notice to end a tenancy; its date is count_days(next_period_end, -N).

Under every reading the landlord may end the tenancy on that notice: it "may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57), and no reason is named. Say so, so the tenant knows what refusing can lead to.

The tenant's choices:

- Pay the new rent. See "If the tenant already paid it" for what paying may mean.
- Pay the old rent and say in writing why. See "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent".
- End the tenancy: load lease_ending. The last day to give notice is count_days(period_end, -N), or count_days(next_period_end, -N) if that has passed.

## Option 4: retaliation

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)).

All of these must be met.

1. **Something the tenant did first.** "Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where:" (83.64(1)) they complained to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), took part in a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), complained to the landlord under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), ended a lease as a servicemember (83.64(1)(d)), paid rent to an association after its demand (83.64(1)(e)), or used fair housing rights (83.64(1)(f)). Fair housing law itself is outside this tool. Another step, like an ordinary repair request: not settled. One: the list is only examples, so it can count. The other: it counts only if it is like the named ones, and a request that says nothing about ending the lease is not 83.56(1)'s complaint.
2. **Good faith.** "In order for the tenant to raise the defense of retaliatory conduct, the tenant must have acted in good faith." (83.64(1)). "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). Applying that is for a court.
3. **Treated differently.** "“Discrimination” under this section means that a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)). Set what they know of other tenants' rent beside the words. The same increase for everyone points against it; say so plainly. If they do not know, say that is the fact to find out.
4. **Primarily because of the complaint.** This is the landlord's motive, for a court. An increase that followed a complaint is not retaliation for that reason alone. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

What it gives: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)), unless "the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)). So not paying the new rent can weaken it; say so.

What the tenant can do about an increase alone, before any case: not settled. One: 83.64(2) makes it only a defense, so there is nothing to raise until a case. The other: 83.64(1) makes the increase unlawful, "Any right or duty declared in this part is enforceable by civil action." (83.54), and a party may recover damages for a failure to comply with "this part" (83.55).

## If the tenant already paid it

"if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).

Ask what they knew when they paid, and set it beside "actual knowledge" (83.56(5)(a)). Whether paying a raised rent gives up the extra, or changes the rent from then on, is not settled. One: paying with knowledge gives up a suit over those months and may show the tenant agreed. The other: an increase the lease never allowed is not rent "due" (83.43(12)), a clause requiring a signed change still stands, and the extra can be claimed under 83.55, with each later month a "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool; do not total them.

## If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent

- **A written demand.** "If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(3)). This tool does not count those days; the demand states them. Say not to ignore it.
- **Taking the old rent.** A landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). So taking it does not mean the landlord gave in. "If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must:" (83.56(5)(a)) give a receipt with the date, the amount, and the balance before filing; or put the amount in the court's registry on filing; or post a new 3-day notice (83.56(5)(a)). Whether the lease's rent is "partial" at all is the dispute.
- **No court case, no removal.** "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)).
- **A case filed.** Say this first. The tenant must pay into the registry "the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon." (83.60(2)). When the amount is what they dispute, the motion is the way to say so: "If a motion to determine rent is filed, documentation in support of the allegation that the rent as alleged in the complaint is in error is required." (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits "only that portion of the full rent for which they are responsible" (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)).
- **Defenses.** The tenant "may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable, that he or she may have, including the defense of retaliatory conduct in accordance with s. 83.64" (83.60(1)(a)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating a notice period or a cap for rent increases as the law.
- Saying a landlord may raise the rent during a set term with no clause and no agreement, or calling the lease's own rent steps an increase.
- Treating 83.57's 30 days as settled for an increase, saying flatly that no notice is needed, or saying flatly that a letter alone changes the rent with no set end date.
- Saying an increase is retaliation because it followed a complaint, or leaving out good faith or being treated differently.
- Telling a tenant they can stop paying rent altogether, explaining a case without 83.60(2), or giving a calendar date for its 5 days.
- Applying a local rent rule from memory.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

tool_calls.name: get_statute_section
tool_calls.result: 83.64 Retaliatory conduct. — (1) It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant. In order for the tenant to raise the defense of retaliatory conduct, the tenant must have acted in good faith. Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where: (a) The tenant has complained to a governmental agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a building, housing, or health code of a suspected violation applicable to the premises; (b) The tenant has organized, encouraged, or participated in a tenant organization; (c) The tenant has complained to the landlord pursuant to s. 83.56 (1); (d) The tenant is a servicemember who has terminated a rental agreement pursuant to s. 83.682 ; (e) The tenant has paid rent to a condominium, cooperative, or homeowners’ association after demand from the association in order to pay the landlord’s obligation to the association; or (f) The tenant has exercised his or her rights under local, state, or federal fair housing laws. (2) Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession. (3) In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause. Examples of good cause include, but are not limited to, good faith actions for nonpayment of rent, violation of the rental agreement or of reasonable rules, or violation of the terms of this chapter. (4) “Discrimination” under this section means that a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct. History. — s. 8, ch. 83-151; s. 450, ch. 95-147; s. 3, ch. 2003-72; s. 15, ch. 2013-136.

tool_calls.name: get_statute_section
tool_calls.result: 83.57 Termination of tenancy without specific term. — A tenancy without a specific duration, as defined in s. 83.46 (2) or (3), may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4), as follows: (1) When the tenancy is from year to year, by giving not less than 60 days’ notice prior to the end of any annual period; (2) When the tenancy is from quarter to quarter, by giving not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any quarterly period; (3) When the tenancy is from month to month, by giving not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period; and (4) When the tenancy is from week to week, by giving not less than 7 days’ notice prior to the end of any weekly period. History. — s. 2, ch. 73-330; s. 3, ch. 81-190; s. 15, ch. 83-217; s. 2, ch. 2023-314.

answer:
**You can fight this, and you have a short deadline. The lease sets your rent at $1,050, and you never agreed to $1,200. Part II (Florida's residential landlord-tenant law) has no section that lets a landlord raise rent alone during a set lease term. The law also gives you only 5 days after service to protect your defenses, so act now.**

The 5 days run from the date you were served (May 5), skipping Saturdays, Sundays, and court holidays. To protect your defenses, you must either pay the rent into the court's registry or file a motion asking the court to decide how much rent is owed. If you do neither, you lose every defense except payment. The landlord can then get an immediate judgment, and you would be removed. I can't give you the calendar date, so read the summons, which should state the requirement. The court clerk's office can also tell you how to file.

Keep paying $1,050 on time. Keep proof of each payment, and bring your lease and those records to court.

Have you filed anything with the court or paid anything into the court since you were served?

DETAILS

### Can the landlord raise your rent during the lease?
- Your lease runs through July 31, 2026. The $1,200 was to start March 1, 2026, which is before the lease ends. That makes this an increase during a set term.
- Lease §4 says: "Rent is $1,050.00 per month." Nothing in the lease lets the landlord raise the rent during the term.
- Lease §10 says the lease "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant." You told me you signed nothing and did not agree.
- Part II has no section letting a landlord raise rent mid-term on its own. So the rent you owe is $1,050.
- Part II also has no rule on how much notice an increase needs or how high it may go. That does not matter here, because the issue is a change during the lease.

### Did paying $1,050 hurt you?
- You paid the lease's rent, not the new rent. That is not paying a raised rent, so it does not look like agreeing to it.
- A landlord who accepts part of the rent does not give up the right to evict or sue over the rest (83.56(5)(a)). Your landlord can therefore still file even though the office took your payments. Whether $1,050 is "partial" rent is exactly what you and the landlord dispute.

### What does the court case require of you?
- Section 83.60(2) says a tenant who raises "any defense other than payment" must pay into the registry "the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due."
- It also says failing to pay "or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment." The landlord is then "entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing."
- Since you dispute the amount, the motion to determine rent is the usual way to say so. The statute requires "documentation in support of the allegation that the rent as alleged in the complaint is in error." Your lease and your payment records are that documentation.
- Whether your defense counts as "payment" or as "another defense" can matter for the registry rule. I can't settle that for you, so the motion protects you either way.

### What defenses can you raise?
- Section 83.60(1)(a) lets you raise "any other defense, whether legal or equitable." Your defense is that the lease sets the rent at $1,050, you paid it, and no rent is owed.
- The winner in the case may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48).

### The written demand
- The landlord's April 20 demand for $300 was the 3-day notice for unpaid rent (83.56(3)). Because you owed no more than $1,050, you can argue the demand was for rent that was not due.
